We probably also want this for Cholesky factors:

multiply_self_transpose(L) = L * L'

and this for general multivariate distros:

multiply_wrap_transpose(y,Sigma) = y' * Sigma * y

or even

normal_thingy(mu,y,SigmaInv) = (y - mu)' * SigmaInv * (y - mu)

implemented with special vari. But then we should just
vectorize all of multi_normal.

- Bob

A special vari to handle a Mahalanobis norm/distance is probably a
good idea, separate from the vectorized multi_normal. It will be
handy in efficiently implementing any elliptical distribution, like
the multivariate student t distribution. That said, I don't think it
will be much faster than the existing multi_normal code for the
non-vectorized case.

sure who did that, it might have even been me...

You added a version with a vectorized y in
multi_normal(y|mu,Sigma) by letting y be a matrix.

The "new" style of vectorization is much more involved
and supports arbitrary subsets of the arguments being
vectorized and/or agrad vars.

Multivariate normals may be a problem, though, in that
we won't be able to easily compute the gradients (or maybe
they're easier than I suspect?).

- Bob

On Tue, Sep 11, 2012 at 5:37 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 11, 2012 5:22:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> Multivariate normals may be a problem, though, in that
>> we won't be able to easily compute the gradients (or maybe
>> they're easier than I suspect?).
>
>
> The gradient wrt mu is not bad. The gradient wrt the primitive parameters
> underlying Sigma is more difficult, especially considering that
> multi_normal() wouldn't know how Sigma was constructed.
>

We could vectorize multi_normal_cholesky first and write the
vectorized mult_normal in terms of that. The derivatives wrt L should
be more straight forward in the cholesky form. Both cases would need
to rely on the identities

d inv(A) = - inv(A) * dA * inv(A)

and

d log(det(A)) = Tr(inv(A) dA)

for matrix A. Given those both forms should be relatively straight forward.

Also, on a side note about vectorizing things. For large N

for (i = 1:N) {
a += foo(b[i])
}

is *much* slower than

vector[N] tmp;

for (i = 1:N) {
tmp[i] = foo(b[i]);
}

a += sum(tmp);

This is true regardless of the complexity of foo(). The extra
allocation and assignment operations are cheap compared to the N extra
vari instantiations implied by the repeated += operations. This is
probably not true with a is not a variable.

This applies equally well for a model or for a vectorized
implementation of a function.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: vectorizing with sum() vs. repeated +=
parts:
On 9/11/12 7:10 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

> Also, on a side note about vectorizing things. For large N
>
> for (i = 1:N) {
> a += foo(b[i])
> }
>
> is *much* slower than
>
> vector[N] tmp;
>
> for (i = 1:N) {
> tmp[i] = foo(b[i]);
> }
>
> a += sum(tmp);
>
> .. The extra

> allocation and assignment operations are cheap compared to the N extra
> vari instantiations implied by the repeated += operations. This is
> probably not true with a is not a variable.

Right -- the speed's from not allocating vari objects and
having to visit them and call their virtual functions during
derivative propagation.

I just dropped a note to that effect in the manual section
on vectorization.

I've thought about this issue before (though not so far
as to vectorize it with sum()), and I think we can
probably use an expression template for the result
of += to lazily drop a sequence of += into a vector sum.

By concentrating on +=, we wouldn't need to
do tons of overloads and conversions as we would with
a more full template expression approach.

sum_expression& operator+=(sum_expression&, var&);

sum_expression& operator+=(var&, var&);

and then we'd need a copy constructor for var
to create the vectorized sum:

var(sum_expression);

> This applies equally well for a model or for a vectorized
> implementation of a function.

Exactly the same principle.

- Bob

>
> I've thought about this issue before (though not so far

> probably use an expression template for the result

>
> sum_expression& operator+=(sum_expression&, var&);
>
> sum_expression& operator+=(var&, var&);
>
> and then we'd need a copy constructor for var
> to create the vectorized sum:
>
> var(sum_expression);

I'm not sure that would work because the return type of operator+= is
generally ignored unless someone does (a += b) += c or d = (a += b) or
something similarly obtuse and strange. In fact, += has to be defined
as a member function:

class var {
...
var &operator+=(const var &b);
...
}

so it can't change the type of the LHS of a += expression. Rather, we
would need a sum vari which can have a variable size and have things
added to it. I think this would break the rules of a vari as it's
value cannot change once its instantiated.

I think the key here is to just write smart C++ code taking this into
account. In terms of all the "lp__ +=" operations in a model, we
could just as easily push the RHS of those statements into a vector
and then call a single sum at the end. (I'm not sure if I've
impemented the sum vari operation to handle a vector<var> type, but
that shouldn't be too hard.

Cheers,
Marcus

You can define it outside of the class, but in some sense
it still behaves like a member function. I really find

type but not in argument types. So we'd have to make
the lp__ accumulator of type sum_expression throughout.

> would need a sum vari which can have a variable size and have things

We could certainly generate smarter C++ code from stanc, if that's
what you mean. I was trying to figure out how to do it
on the C++ API side.

But we can't just accumulate because users can access intermediate
results, even for lp__. Maybe we could restrict that and instead
of treating lp__ as a variable users have access to, force them
to use something like an increment_lp(real) function.

- Bob

to do something other than increment lp__ and not really coming up

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] vectorizing with sum() vs. repeated +=
parts:
On 9/13/12 4:17 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Personally, I'm comfortable just telling people to use vectorized
> functions. If it's good enough for R/Matlab/Python/Octave/everything
> else it's good enough for me. But that's just because it seems easier
> to me, which maybe it's not.

The only problem is where there's not already an array
over which you want to vectorize.

In the current example, there's a running sum and allocating something
to put it into in order to vectorize is a pain and
makes the models hard to read (just the opposite of
the usual vectorization use case, which can make the
models easier to read).

Now if the loop-index-dependent function foo(n,...) can itself
be vectorized, then that's ideal.

> On a related note, I wonder if we could make something like an apply()
> function that compiles to something efficient? That could be an
> alternative to vectorizing every function we've got, but then again it
> might be more work than it's worth.

We could do the apply, but the question would be how to
implement it so that it vectorized rather than just looping.
The issue isn't just moving from Stan to C++, but moving
the += over var to the vectorized vari impl.

- Bob
